items.paragraph: It seems obvious that famines happen when there is not enough food. What collapsed was not the harvest but the ability of particular groups to obtain food: labourers whose wages fell, artisans whose customers vanished, herders whose animals lost value as grain prices rose. A famine, on this view, is less a shortage of food than a failure of access to it, concentrated on those whose means of buying or growing it have broken down. items.paragraph: Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. items.paragraph: Schools that pair older pupils with younger ones for tutoring usually set out to help the younger children, and they often do. The gain comes from the effort of explanation, and schools that want it must design tutoring so that explanation is actually required.

items.paragraph: Atlases encourage us to see rivers as natural boundaries: a blue line on the map separates one province or country from the next, and it is tempting to assume the line was drawn there because the water divided people. For most of history the reverse was closer to the truth. Before railways, moving goods by water was far cheaper than moving them by land, so a river bound the communities along its banks into a single zone of trade, kinship and shared speech, while the hills on either side were the real obstacles. Rivers became frontiers largely when states, wanting lines that were easy to describe in treaties and to defend, chose them for that purpose. The division we read into the landscape is therefore often an administrative choice laid over a geography that once worked the other way. This is not to deny that some rivers, wide or violent, have always separated peoples.

items.paragraph: Planting vast areas with a single, genetically uniform variety of a crop makes farming efficient: every plant ripens at the same time, responds to the same fertiliser and can be harvested by the same machine. The same uniformity, however, creates a hidden vulnerability. The efficiency of uniformity is visible every season; its risk appears rarely, but when it does, it can arrive all at once.

items.paragraph: A standard textbook argument holds that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment, since employers buy less of anything that becomes more expensive. items.paragraph: Listeners asked to rate recorded speakers often judge those with certain accents as less competent, even when the words spoken are identical. It is tempting to read this as simple prejudice against particular regions or classes, and partly it is. But some of the effect has a duller source: listeners find an unfamiliar accent harder to process, and the extra effort of understanding is easily misattributed to the speaker, as if a message that was hard to follow had been less clearly thought. This matters because the two explanations call for different remedies. Prejudice must be confronted; mere unfamiliarity tends to shrink with exposure, so that a listener who hears an accent regularly may stop penalising it without ever having examined an attitude.

items.paragraph: When a writer dies leaving a novel unfinished, or instructs that drafts be destroyed, those who hold the papers face a familiar dilemma. Publishing seems to betray the author's wishes or, at least, to present as a book what the author never judged to be one. Suppressing seems to deprive readers of work that may be among the best the writer produced. The dilemma is usually framed as loyalty against value, but this framing overlooks a third consideration: how the work is presented. An unfinished draft printed as a draft, with its gaps visible and its status made plain, misrepresents the author far less than the same text smoothed by an editor into the appearance of completion. The question is not only whether to publish but in what form.

items.paragraph: Ask people why they chose one pair of socks over another, why they liked a job candidate, why they moved house, and they will readily give reasons. It is tempting to treat these reasons as reports, read off from some inner record of what actually moved them. There is good ground for doubt. People's explanations often match what an outsider would guess, given the culture's ordinary theories of why people act, more closely than they match whatever in fact influenced the choice; and when an influence was something they did not notice, such as the position of an item on a shelf, they seldom mention it. It does not follow that people know nothing of their own minds. They are usually right about what they feel and what they are attending to. What is shaky is their access to the causes of their choices, which they seem to infer much as anyone else would, while experiencing the inference as direct knowledge.
